done.why: I typed south toward the skeleton's room for one more go at the maze and the world told me I had taken all 150 turns it allows. I was mid-loop, with a leaflet and a bottle for markers and a strong suspicion the maze was built to keep returning me to its mouth.

about: It is the old white-house-and-cellar game, the one with the mailbox and the grue, but somebody has gone through it with a dry wit and a taste for the morbid. Underneath the familiar errands (lamp, sword, rug, troll, egg, painting) it is about a maze that is not simply confusing but openly uninterested in you, where everything you examine (the skeleton, his dead lantern, the honest dead end, the knife rust forgot to touch) is a little essay on people who came down here and did not come back up. The knife killed me for pointing it at a corpse, and the game shrugged and scattered my things across the Empire. It is about being one more luckless adventurer, told with affection.

moments.note: The window is 'slightly ajar' but closing it says it is 'already closed'.
'squeeze through the window' got 'You can't see any such thing' with the window right there and just opened.
'Only Santa Claus climbs down chimneys.'
The gothic lettering translates to 'This space intentionally left blank.'
Examining the barred trap door from below gave a real, specific description: planks, iron bands, no handle or ring on this side.
The troll gleefully ate the garlic I offered instead of fighting.
The maze wall is 'solid, plain and entirely uninterested in you.'
Listening in the maze: the same silence as everywhere else, 'which is no help at all.'
Blundered 'up' straight into the skeleton and its hoard.
Touching the rusty knife made my sword pulse once with blinding blue light. A warning I ignored.
'The rust has not touched the edge. That is not a thing rust usually overlooks.'
Stabbing the skeleton with the knife turned the blade on my own throat. Dead, revived in a forest, belongings scattered, lamp tidied back to the living room.
My sword turned up north of the house; later the bag of coins was in the artist's studio. The scattering was real and findable.
The tidy somebody had left my lamp burning: 'It is already on.'
The chasm: a dark my lamp 'does not so much light as annoy.'
The chimney has room for 'you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.' A rule stated plainly and gracefully.
On a brief re-entry the skeleton was not listed and I thought it had gone; a 'look' showed it still there.
The dead man's lantern: batteries 'gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things.'
A one-way drop with a warning that I would not be able to get back up; I took it anyway.
The dead end is 'the one honest thing in the place: it does not pretend to go anywhere.'
I walked east into the dead end but west did not lead back out.
Forty-odd turns in the maze and nearly every path looped me back to the leaflet at the entrance. I never found the grating or a second way out.

wished: Pry the boards off the front door, or do anything at all to them; the parser did not know the sentence.
Squeeze through the window as I phrased it, rather than having to say 'enter window'.
Cut the rug with the sword, or use the sword on anything that was not the troll.
Smell things; 'listen' and 'examine' in the maze had lovely answers and 'smell' was unrecognised.
Say 'wander' in a maze and have it mean something.
Mark maze rooms more cheaply; I only had a leaflet and a bottle to drop and ran out of markers.
Find the grating or any exit from the maze other than the mouth I came in by.
Open the egg, or at least be told what tools and expertise would do it.

lines.line: Only Santa Claus climbs down chimneys.
lines.why: The first sign the world would answer a silly request in kind rather than with a shrug.

lines.line: High overhead is the underside of the trap door: rough planks and iron bands, and not a handle or a ring to be had from this side.
lines.why: I examined a thing most games leave blank and got a real answer; it told me the rewrite reached into corners.

lines.line: Whatever he came into the maze looking for, the maze found him first.
lines.why: It set the tone for the whole maze and, in hindsight, for what happened to me a few turns later.

lines.line: The rust has not touched the edge. That is not a thing rust usually overlooks.
lines.why: A warning dressed as description. I read it, admired it, and stabbed the skeleton anyway.

lines.line: Your belongings, such as they were, have not come with you. They are scattered about the Empire, though somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: Death handled with humour and with consequences I could actually track: I found the sword, the bottle, the axe and the bag again.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.
lines.why: The best single sentence I read; it made the lamp feel small.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: A restriction stated so exactly that I knew what to drop without guessing.

lines.line: Its batteries gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things.
lines.why: Grim, funny, and a quiet reminder that my own lamp is on a clock.

lines.line: It is the one honest thing in the place: it does not pretend to go anywhere.
lines.why: The maze speaking about itself, and admitting what it was doing to me.

fun.why: Feeding the troll garlic, dying by my own hand with a cursed knife, finding my scattered things again and climbing out of a chimney into the kitchen were all genuinely good fun; the maze ate the last third and gave less back.

engagement.why: I never wanted to stop; the examine responses kept paying out and the death did not break my momentum, it sent me on an errand. The maze loops were the only stretch where I was moving on habit rather than curiosity.

difficulty.why: The house and troll were easy once I stopped being clever; the knife killed me in one go with fair warning I ignored; the maze was the hard part and I could not crack it in forty turns with only two markers. About right for a first visit, though the maze leaned hard.

interestingness.why: The familiar bones are there, but every object I looked closely at had something new and pointed to say, and the maze has a personality rather than just being a nuisance. I was never sure what had changed and what had not, which kept me looking.

prose.why: The added descriptions are the best thing here: dry, exact, a little morbid, never long. The chasm, the dead lantern, the knife and the dead end were all lines I would read aloud to someone.
